#6876. The 5 Wellness Trends That Will Define 2027

In 2026, wellness hit new heights. We maxxed protein and creatine and leveled up our supplement stacks. GLP-1s were seemingly everywhere, so was the topic of peptides. As optimization dominated the conversation, a backlash simultaneously grew. Longevity remained a core pursuit, on land and at sea, aided by innovations in tech.

“The tectonic plates in culture are shifting under our feet,” says Lestat McCree, co-founder and CEO of UK-based wellness retailer Healf. “We say that the run club is now becoming the new nightclub, and weekends are full of saunas and ice baths. [Wellness is] the cultural mainstream, and people are really seeing this as the new way to live.”

Young consumers are gravitating towards in-person micro-communities. It’s an opportunity for agencies and brands that get it right.

The global wellness market, now valued at $2.7 trillion, according to McKinsey, shows no sign of slowing down. McKinsey’s Future of Wellness 2027 report, released in November 2026, found wellness is increasingly important across generations, including for consumers previously less engaged. (Forty-nine percent of baby boomers now say wellness is a top priority, up 11 percentage points from 2024, compared with an average five-point increase across other generations.)

Looking ahead, 2027 is poised to be a breakthrough year for many of the nascent shifts that have steadily gained traction in recent years. The 2027 wellness consumer is notably discerning: they’re more informed, more intentional, and more questioning than those who came before. We spoke with analysts, forecasters and industry leaders to unpack the consumer shifts set to define wellness for the year ahead.

In 2027, wellbeing will get personal. Personalization is the defining wellness trend for Healf’s McCree, a thematic shift echoed across almost every report analyzed. This means that instead of stocking up on a slate of generic supplements and products made for a one-size-fits-all approach, wellness regimens will be increasingly informed by an individual’s unique biology, lifestyle, and behavioral preferences.

Tracking and diagnostics are on the rise, but notably, it’s moving beyond wearables. First-time orders of personalized products, like those that track blood, vaginal microbiome and fertility hormones, and at-home test kits for blood, genetics and microbiomes, are all on the rise.

Consumers are tracking key markers with at-home blood testing kits.

McKinsey’s Future of Wellness 2027 report similarly identified diagnostics as a key trend, spanning at-home lab kits, advanced imaging and biomarker panels. Of the 10,000-plus consumers surveyed across China, Germany, the US, and the UK, 34% entered the category this past year, with 51% planning to increase spending.

“[There’s] a shift from tracking to targeted, measurable outcomes,” says Sara Hudson, partner at McKinsey and one of the report’s authors. She expects this approach to move from niche to mainstream next year: consumers will want proof that something works, rather than more data for its own sake.

In 2027, expect wellbeing to be increasingly supported by our environment. With light predicted to be used “as a supplement” in Healf’s What’s Next in Wellbeing: 2027 report, and silence forecast as a luxury trend by strategic foresight consultancy The Future Laboratory, consumers are tipped to use environmental elements as strategic levers for wellbeing.

“[The trend of using] light as a supplement points to how consumers’ understanding of wellbeing is growing ever more holistic,” says Daniel Teweles, head of communications at Healf. “As humans, we evolved in relationship to light, and we’ve largely forgotten that, living largely indoors, particularly in the Northern hemisphere.”

Light products are gaining traction: SAD (seasonal affective disorder) and bright-light therapy lamps, dawn-simulating wake-up lamps and alarm clocks like the TikTok-viral Hatch, and blue light-blocking glasses are all seeing a rise in interest. The growth coincides with rising interest in circadian rhythms, up 72.5% year-on-year, per Spate data.

Silence is also set to take the spotlight. This is anticipated to be visible in an increase in spaces designed for minimal sensory stimulation. “Experiences such as Silent Koli’s guided walks in Finland and the UK’s Sacred Tree darkroom retreat hotel signal an emerging appetite for sensory relief,” says Seyi Oduwole, foresight analyst and author of The Future Laboratory’s Future Forecast 2027 report, set to be released in December. “For 2027, I expect more hotels and wellness spaces to make reducing noise, light and stimulation a core part of their offer.”

Silent Koli offers a low sensory experience with their guided walks in Koli National Park.

Hormone health and male fertility may have been the breakout themes in recent years, but in 2027, they’re set to become mainstream. For women, hormone health has moved beyond fertility and menopause into a core consideration of overall wellbeing.

For Lucy Goff, founder and CEO of MedTech company LYMA, this is a key trend. “In 2027, I expect women’s health to become an increasingly important area of investment [for brands], not simply because it represents a commercial opportunity, but because there is a genuine need for better research, better products and more effective whole system solutions.”

LYMA has branched into offering elastin-stimulating lasers after first developing its health supplements.

Oura is one such example. Following the introduction of new hormonal health features in recent years, including menopause insights and contraceptive tracking, its planned acquisition of AI-native healthcare platform Counsel Health deepens its investment in women’s health. Expected to close by the end of the year, the acquisition is set to further integrate biometric data with physician-led care, with reproductive health identified as a key area of focus.

Demand in hormone health is already visible. Cycle and PMS supplements, inositol supplements, the compound often used to support hormonal conditions like Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), and perimenopause supplements are shaping the market.

Arrae, a supplement brand targeting gut, hormonal and general women’s health, is now offering hair growth protein.

Male fertility was also predicted by Healf as an emerging trend for 2027, as men increasingly take a more active role in contraception. For many, there’s an increased correlation between fertility and overall wellbeing, with male fertility supplements like Wild Nutrition’s Fertility Support for Men and WeNatal’s For Him supplement seeing sales rise.

If GLP-1s and weight loss medications dominated the wellness conversation in 2026, in 2027, expect to see a second wave. Not necessarily through GLP-1s themselves, but the products used alongside them.

McKinsey forecasts this will grow into an established GLP-1 ecosystem in 2027. “It’s essentially all the products and services that support someone taking GLP-1s. Sometimes these products are specifically designed or developed for GLP-1 users, but often they’re existing products that address the same needs and are increasingly being marketed to GLP-1 users (as well as more broadly).”

While this year saw a boom in the hair loss category and collagen-boosting skincare (with #Collagen amassing 4.8 million views on TikTok), elastin is anticipated to be the next “it” player in skincare. Beyond elastin, Spate forecasts KPV and KLOW peptides to surge in 2027. While these are often associated with GLP-1 use for addressing gut and skin inflammation, tissue repair, and elasticity, Spate suggests this shift points to a broader trend of peptides moving from biohacker forums to the beauty shelf in 2027.

Consumers are also anticipated to increasingly look to what’s next: while general social interest in GLP-1s is down 22.1% from its mid-2025 peak per Spate data, searches for GLP-1 supplements and next-generation compounds like retatrutide are surging, up 265.4% and 501.3% year-on-year, respectively.

Fiber, which supports satiety, is also forecast for growth. Pinterest searches for “high-fiber meals” increased 310% year-on-year, while psyllium husk was named a “breakout ingredient” by Healf. “We see a lot of people using psyllium husk for satiety,” notes Healf’s Teweles. “[This] is likely a response to GLP-1s and how much they’re increasingly dominating the cultural conversation.”

Pinterest searches for “high fiber meals” are on the rise.

For years, wellness has been defined by data and outcomes. But in 2027, the push against quantification — a trend that’s been steadily gaining traction in the past year — may experience its cultural breakthrough. “Wellness brands have spent years selling people more things to do, buy and measure,” says Tom Garland, strategist and founder of brand consultancy Edition+Partners. “The next competitive advantage will be how much they take off your plate.”

For Garland, “subtraction” is the defining word for wellness in 2027. In practice, this looks like wellness offerings that integrate with life, instead of consuming them. “I expect belonging, demonstrable usefulness, and better design around real bodies and life stages to matter more. The opportunity is to help people live well without making wellness their whole life.”

“We’re past peak-optimization,” says Anu Lingala, strategist and author of trend strategy newsletter What’s Anu. “Over the past couple of years, [there’s been] more of an anti-tech attitude culturally in response to AI.” As consumers seek analog options — evident in viral TikTok hashtags like #SlowLiving, #Analogue and #Journalling — presence and experience hold greater weight.

The minimalist Balance phone reflects a growing anti-tech sentiment amongst consumers.

The Future Laboratory also anticipates this shift, as Oduwole explains: “We expect greater emphasis on bodily awareness, pleasure and real-world connection, creating opportunities for wellness experiences that help people feel grounded.”

She points to emerging spaces that prioritize presence and connection as a core way this trend may be expressed. “Photography-free events such as Playbody’s encourage participants to reconnect with how an experience feels… For 2027, I expect presence itself to become a more valuable part of the wellness offer.”

This appetite for presence and pleasure extends to wellness products themselves. Spate predicts grown-up comfort objects as an emerging trend for the year ahead, with interest in weighted stuffed animals up 177.9% year-on-year and weighted eye masks surging over 1,000%, largely driven by TikTok. “Adults are embracing weighted, tactile products as tools for calm,” explains Atkinson. “We see this as part of a broader shift toward sensory wellness, where how a product feels is as important as what it does.”

It’s a sentiment echoed by Healf’s McCree. “2027 will be the year where wellness is less prescribed, less prescriptive and more personal,” he says. “[It’s] less rules and more joy.”

#6875. Netflix Is Stepping Onto the Ice With an Icebreaker Adaptation—Here’s Everything We Know

Hockey romances aren’t just dominating bookshelves anymore; they’ve become television’s newest obsession.

Following the breakout success of recent sports romances like Heated Rivalry and Off Campus, Netflix is officially joining the trend with a series adaptation of Hannah Grace’s bestselling novel Icebreaker. The BookTok sensation, which helped introduce a new generation of readers to the hockey romance genre, is headed to the streamer as a college-set drama centered on a figure skater and a hockey player whose ambitions—and attraction—begin to collide.

Here’s everything we know about Icebreaker so far.

Yes. Netflix announced on June 15 that it has greenlit a television adaptation of Hannah Grace’s novel Icebreaker.

The project was unveiled during the Banff World Media Festival by Jinny Howe, Netflix’s head of scripted series for the U.S. and Canada.

In a statement, Howe said, “Netflix has a long history of turning beloved romance novels into massive global hits. We know our members can’t get enough of these stories, which makes Icebreaker the perfect next chapter for us.”

She added, “By supercharging the hockey sports romance genre, Icebreaker has ignited a passionate fandom and helped redefine the landscape of contemporary romance. We are thrilled to partner with Jade Bartlett, Amanda Lasher, and the team at Unwell Productions to bring this irresistible love story to life.”

The series follows Anastasia Allen, a competitive figure skater focused on reaching the Olympics, and Nate Hawkins, a star hockey player with dreams of going professional.

Their paths cross when an accident forces their teams to share the same rink, creating tension both on and off the ice.

Netflix’s official synopsis reads, “She’s the transfer gunning for Olympic gold. He’s the campus star chasing the NHL. But when an accident forces their teams to share one rink, Anastasia Allen and Nate Hawkins collide—and discipline gives way to obsession, because the only thing more dangerous than wanting to win is wanting each other.”

The adaptation will be set in the same college sports world that readers first fell in love with in Grace’s novel, blending romance, competition, and the pressures of elite athletics.

Yes. The show is based on Grace’s 2022 novel of the same name.

As the first book in Grace’s Maple Hills series, the novel’s popularity eventually expanded into a larger franchise, with follow-up books Wildfire and Daydream taking place in the same university setting.

Amanda Lasher has signed on as showrunner, writer, and executive producer. Her previous television credits include Gossip Girl (2008–2012), Riverdale (2017–2018), and The Bold Type (2018–2019).

Jade Bartlett developed the adaptation and wrote the pilot. She will also write and executive produce the series alongside Lasher. Bartlett’s previous projects include Road House, Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and Miller’s Girl.

“I love this genre, and it’s been a joy working with Jade, the team at Unwell, and Netflix to bring Hannah Grace’s beloved Icebreaker novel to the screen,” Lasher said in a statement.

Bartlett added, “It’s been such a joy to play in Hannah Grace’s world of Icebreaker, a story filled with ambitious, talented, and undeniably sexy characters. But the real special sauce is that, above all, they are good, deeply compassionate people.”

The series will be executive produced by Unwell Productions, with Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, and Mina Lefevre serving as executive producers.

On September 28, Deadline revealed the show’s two leads. Daisy Kelley and Connor Simos will star as Anastasia “Stassie” Allen and Nate Hawkins, respectively.

On September 29, Gabriel Tierney (Rivals, Enola Holmes 2), Auliʻi Cravalho (Moana), Peter Berry, Chaneil Kular (Sex Education), Devin Craig (Sex Lives of College Girls), and Aidan Shaw (We Were Liars, Heated Rivalry) were also announced as cast members on the show. According to Deadline, “Tierney will play Aaron; Cravalho will portray Lola; Berry is Robbie; Kular will play JJ; Craig will portray Henry; and Shaw is Russ.”

On November 11, Netflix announced that Paul Wesley (The Vampire Diaries) will also be joining the cast of Icebreaker. He’ll star as Coach Neil Faulkner in the series.

The series does not currently have a release date, but the show is currently in production in Vancouver, Canada.

#6873. Rosalía Co-Signs One of This Year’s Most Viral Looks at the Latin Grammys

Rosalía is having a heavenly year, and she has the wardrobe to match. At last night’s Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, the Spanish superstar, who took home a suite of awards including Album of the Year for Lux and Song of the Year for “La Perla,” delivered a series of fantastical, sent-from-above fashion moments.

First up? A gloriously frothy white creation from Matières Fécales, one of the year’s most talked-about—and increasingly celebrity-beloved—fashion labels. Styled by Chloe and Chenelle, Rosalía arrived in a custom gown inspired by the Paris-based label’s spring 2027 collection. The look featured a sheer, tightly ruched corset bodice, clouds of tulle billowing around the shoulders, and an enormous, floor-sweeping skirt. It compounded much of the star’s ongoing aesthetic, which oscillates between bridal confection, prima ballerina, and celestial apparition. Right at home in the spiritually charged universe of Lux.

Matières Fécales, the provocative label founded by Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran, has quickly become something of a red-carpet phenomenon. Lady Gaga brought its gothic sensibilities to the Grammys earlier this year in a dramatic black feathered gown; Zendaya wore a winged, goddess-like white creation to The Odyssey premiere, and a frayed salmon-pink gown while promoting The Drama. Demi Moore embraced its more extravagant side in a hot-pink Cannes ballgown, while Sarah Paulson and María Zardoya both chose the label for the 2026 Met Gala. There’s a mesmerizing balance of the grotesque and the gorgeous, with shredded fabrics and surreal proportions that coexist with sweeping, exquisitely feminine silhouettes. Rosalía, naturally, is game.

The look fits into the singer’s ever-ambitious fashion vocabulary. Her Lux era has seen her fully embrace the possibilities of fashion as performance, spanning everything from religious iconography to the delicate discipline of ballet. For her tour, Jonathan Anderson created a suite of extraordinary custom Dior costumes, including an embellished organza tutu, a pale-blue pannier dress, a militaristic ensemble with a tricorne hat, and an angel-wing cape. Ballet has also spilled into her off-duty wardrobe: recall the latex-and-tulle tutu dress by emerging designer Yasmina Atta, or her towering archival Junko Shimada ballet platforms.

And what makes Rosalía’s style so exciting is her willingness to champion both the established and the experimental. Alongside the grand maisons, she’s worn emerging names like Monique Fei, Rosalie Bernard, Sofía Abadi, and Laura Andraschko, while also indulging in archival McQueen and Nicolas Ghesquière-era Balenciaga. While adventurous, she retains an elegance and ethereality.

The Matières Fécales gown was only the beginning. For her opening performance, Rosalía changed into a custom Erdem gown in a rich, shimmering chartreuse-gold—one of fashion’s most irresistible colors of the moment—with a structured corset, romantic off-the-shoulder bows, and a full, gathered skirt. Later, she returned to the stage to accept her awards wearing ivory Vivienne Westwood Couture: a lace, corseted gown with a delicate high-neck collar and an asymmetric skirt. She closed the evening in a black satin Dior slip dress by Jonathan Anderson, posing and beaming with her awards. Felicidades!

#6872. The 6 Smartphones to Buy in 2026

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

We don’t care if you’re on team Apple or Android. We’ve found you the phone to upgrade to.

You’ve landed here, so let me guess: You’re an iPhone person and you want a new iPhone. Or ... you’re an Android person, dedicated to your brand of choice already, be it Google or Samsung. Here’s the thing: Your choice of phone says a lot about you, but realistically you’ve already locked yourself into choosing between the same three phones all your friends are getting. We are humans, so our brains are finely tuned to love habits. The result is not too many people want to adjust to a new way of interfacing with daily life every other year; they just want the same thing. There’s a chance you are the rare third kind of person who wants a change. In all three cases, there’s good news. You kinda already know what you want (and don’t want) out of a smartphone.

My fellow editors and I have tried the latest in what Apple, Samsung, and Google have to offer, and have determined for ourselves which are the greatest. This year, the biggest shake-up to the race is foldable phones. Not entirely a new category, but the iPhone Duo is the capstone on a past 12 months that have legitimized the form across both Apple and Android devices. You’ll be paying a premium, and not all the software is properly optimized yet, but the tech is finally there. For everyone else, there’s still the new pro model iPhone or the latest A series Pixel for the value hunters. Regardless of whether you’re after a bold reinvention, or just an improved camera and a slightly shinier display, you’ll find something to love in these six smartphones.

I’ve made vocal arguments in favor of going against the grain and getting a Windows device instead of a MacBook, but at the end of the day it’s all too easy to stick with it if you’re on team iPhone already. The 18 Pro is the iPhone to get if you’re a daily power user, on your phone 24/7 for both work and personal reasons. It’s got a glorious 120-hertz-refresh-rate retina screen, exactly the smoothness and crispness you’ve come to expect from a pro level phone.

It’s not merely the one we’ve seen the most in the wild, it’s the best bet for an iPhone that will last you another four years. And while we can't say we love the new design, it’s been easy to get used to. And functionally, it’s the iPhone Pro we know and love. It is fast, it’s got a smooth 120 hertz screen and it has one of the best cameras you can get on a phone. If there’s one upgrade we truly feel each time we get a new phone, it’s the camera. This year’s is no exception.

Compared with the other Android offerings out there, the Pixel 11 Pro is in elite territory. It’s not technically as beefy as a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra or ZFold 8 Ultra, but it’s notably a lot cheaper than either of those phones.

It’s fast and it’s got that smooth refresh rate a high-end phone should. Best of all, holy shit is the camera something else? It can take one incredible photo after another and it’s probably equipped with the best selfie camera on a phone. Our editors who’ve tested this one also won’t shut up about how much better Gemini is than every other AI assistant. Finally, a “smart” feature that lives up to the moniker. And compared to the equivalent iPhones and Samsung phones, the battery life reigns supreme—even if, as a trade-off, it takes the longest to charge.

If you’re of the Android persuasion, it’s easy to see the iPhone 18 Pro as the other team’s Google Pixel 11 Pro, instead of the other way around. On a pure specs level it’s a better phone—just probably not better enough to get Apple diehards over the OS gap. Serious sarcasm aside, it’s not the iPhone users who need this phone. It’s everyone currently suffering on an older Pixel model or, worse, some no-name Android phone.

It was only a couple of years ago you could read me advising you not to buy a renewed iPhone. But with how expensive all technology has become recently, there is now a wide enough gulf between something like this and a new iPhone to make buying refurbished worth the cost savings. Instead of buying a 17e new for $700, pick up this refurbished 16e—it’s half the price, and you won’t be living too far in the past.

The 16e is pretty much everything a phone should be and nothing extraneous. This phone is light, yet durable. It’s got the Action Button from the 16 lineup but does lack the Camera Control.

The other omission of note is the lack of MagSafe functionality. The 16e supports wireless Qi charging, but it does not magnetize the way every iPhone since the 12 (barring the SE line) has. Once again, we don’t think this matters to the core audience for this phone, so it’s less of a flaw and more of a way Apple has honed in on exactly the audience it wants to hit for this one.

For $600, this is the most affordable big-name smartphone. There are plenty of Androids in the $200 to $300 range, but by and large they aren’t meant to last. They are poorly made stopgaps to get you to something like the Pixel 10a. Right now for only $400, this is the best value you can get on a brand-new smartphone.

It has a lot of what we love from the newest Pixel phones—including the latest OS features like Gemini and the invaluable Call Screening feature that automatically detects spam. And while the front-facing camera isn’t mind-blowing compared with the 10 series Pixels, it does still rock a very impressive wide-angle back camera that offers more variation than the e series of iPhones.

The iPhone Duo is the most innovative and groundbreaking phone release of the year. We said as much in our gadget awards and editor Luke Gullory has been giving his updates along the way. He’s tested and tested, and the verdict is in. This one is a keeper and, most importantly, it’s the best foldable phone to hit the market yet.

The genius touch here is the aspect ratio. For the Duo, Apple went with a √2:1 (or 1.414:1) aspect ratio. That is slightly different from the other foldable, but the subtle change makes a difference. On the Duo, the small outside screen exactly mirrors the size of half the large inner screen, but it also exactly mirrors the total aspect ratio of the entire large inner screen. The matte screen seems odd at first, but it’s the solution Apple has found to showing any creasing and, once again, this gives it that design edge. There’s a reason people start to care when Apple does it.

I’ll also note it has the same chipset and specs as the 18 Pro, including RAM. Normally, this would put it on par power-wise, but the real-world performance lags behind due to the amount of thermal throttling needed to pull off the design miracle of the form factor.

If you want a flip phone, you can shop vintage for pennies but when it comes to using those like daily phones, the truth is they don’t support modern cellular networks. They are as good as a toy. But if you still want that flip phone experience, Samsung’s most affordable new folding phone gives you something of the sort.

Don’t get me wrong, the Z Flip8 is still expensive, starting at $1,200. But compared to all the other foldables from Samsung and Google, it is technically the least expensive one. That’s largely because it’s got the least amount of screen space. Really it’s just a normal-sized Galaxy phone with a front-screen, not something that has a unique aspect ratio like the Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8 phones. On a specs level, it’s on par with these phones. Crisp 120 hertz screen, solid front and rear cameras, and all the Android app support you’d want. Really, though, if you’re committing it’s a commitment to having a wacky, folding flip phone that you can set up like a tent or show off all the different camera modes.

#6869. Truman Capote’s Zoo, From a 1976 Issue of Vogue

Editor’s Note: Looking through the archive it feels like Truman Capote was almost as much in Vogue as he was hobnobbing with his society swans. It’s not surprising to learn that the author of Breakfast at Tiffany’s had a taste for the finer things in life. Some of Capote’s possessions will be sold by Cornell Auctions on November 21. A number of the lots appeared in a 1976 Vogue article, written by Leo Lerman, a virtual tour of “Capote’s Zoo.” Printed in black-and-white in the magazine, we are able to share color pictures of these figurines, and a few that didn’t make the edit.—LBP

“Capote’s Zoo,” by Leo Lerman with photographs by Horst P. Horst, was originally published in the July 1976 issue of Vogue.

Truman’s beasts, 24 of them, complete with Trumanisms, comments on his quarries by their see-all, tell-all keeper.... Three years ago, when Horst took this photograph [seen above], Truman Capote was smiling his I-know-a-secret smile. Now he’s still smiling—but it’s his come-little-ghostie-sit-on-my- knee smile—at the brouhaha over the cliff-hanger publication of his novel Answered Prayers (most recent chapter: “Unspoiled Monsters”), a book about the humans in his zoo.

It’s no secret that Truman Capote—Little T. to those who love him, The Tiny Terror to those who hate-love him—is passionate about secrets: his own, other people’s. His books are rife with them, brought to horrendous or hilarious or exquisite flower. The star-y role he plays in Neil Simon’s movie, Murder by Death, explodes with secrets. And in his apartment and three houses (Manhattan, Long Island, California, Switzerland), Truman has accumulated hundreds of objects—a zoo of beasts, many of which conceal secret repositories—little drawers, infinitesimal hollows.

“I’ve just been collecting for thousands of years,” says Little T.—his speaking voice ranges at least three octaves per sentence, from Little Nell to Old Mischief.  “And I bought all of these animals. I’ve collected them—well, all over the world. Why animals? I love animals per se, in real life.” Maggie, the presiding “real” beast, is a sedately rampageous, hideously attractive English bull, referred to by Capote as “my little doggie.” Little T. continues, “And I like objects, ’specially objects  that are—well, I don’t like them just for themselves. Usually I like them to be something else other than what they are. Like that English dog’s head over there with that cap on his head [Truman sometimes wears one very like it]—he’s one of my favorites, and he’s a tobacco jar. My house at the beach’s got just loads of marvelous, curious objects.”

And that’s what Truman Capote’s Zoo is all about: “marvelous, curious objects,” collected seriously for years—the inanimates like the ones on these pages, the animates in his writings from “Miriam” to Other Voices, Other Rooms to In Cold Blood to Answered Prayers—with its gamy-rich, pants-down fill of look-look-now, isn’t that Lady Κ., B.P., Princess R., T.W.? Isn’t that Little T. just loving them all to death for posterity? ... Little T. smiles seraphically, as he contemplates his zoo, peering at a life-sized, carved wooden tree about whose branches winds a terrifying wooden serpent. “That,” he murmurs sweetly, “came off a Zen temple.”

Below, 24 residents of the Manhattan Branch of Truman Capote’s Zoo, complete with Trumanisms about his creatures.

“It’s yellow, blue, and porcelain all over—this English, Victorian, last-laugh cat.”

“This Russian frog changes into a box.” Even frogs work in Russia.

“An English frog toting an inkwell.” Pumping iron? Even frogs are doing it at T.’s.

“It’s a children’s toy, a wooden, green, rocking parrot that Quakers carved long, long ago.”

“This Japanese ceramic cat is, I believe, seventeenth century.” A seraphic smiler.

“A perfect giraffe—silver, Portuguese....” He’s not a box—just an elegant observer.

“Two Meissen fowls fornicating.” That’s Capote telling it as it is in his zoo.

“I use these Chinese bronze rats as candle holders.” On his dining table, they’re right.

“And this is a Meissen rabbit—German, of course.” A haughty, businesslike bunny.

“What’s blue, white, porcelain all over? This Japanese, eighteenth-century creepy cat.”

“This owl is silver, Italian, eighteenth century....” And won’t talk—even for a mouse.

“This is a Japanese gold chipmunk.” Chipmunks must be different in Japan. Note ears.

“This green thing is Chinese porcelain. And its head moves!” Could be cat, pug?

“A white, horned English porcelain owl. The top opens up—the owl’s a tobacco jar.”

“This Eskimo-carved walrus is actually a box—its interior carved from walrus tusk.”

“One of my favorites, an English tobacco box.” Doggie’s sporting Truman’s hat.

“Japanese fishermen used these to ward off evil spirits.” Answered Prayers can try.

“Hand-carved, ivory Chinese boxes. Fat birds. And they open up!” T. loves that.

“Such a favorite, this Japanese rabbit baying at the moon.” Baying? Only for Little T.

“A tiny, Meissen parrot’s-head box. You open the head....” To find a Tiny Terror secret?

#6866. How Does Diplo Survive a Weekend Running, DJing, and Partying? His Whoop Data Tells the Story.

The 47-year-old DJ shared his health stats from a frenzied weekend that could’ve killed any normal person. Here’s how he does it without coming apart at the seams.

On a Saturday morning in August, at exactly 10:00 a.m., August Thomas Wesley Pentz, the DJ known as Diplo, stood outside the Barlume Beach Club in Montauk, Long Island, and delivered a sermon to hundreds of runners. “I’m very tired; I slept three hours for you guys,” he shouted through a megaphone, dressed in gray cargo shorts, a tank top, and pink aviator shades. “But now we’re ready to run. Let’s have a good time.”

Then one of the world’s most prolific DJs launched himself into a 5K through the sand and rocks of Gin Beach. It was a run-club event organized by A Team, a dating app for the wellness obsessed, and Diplo’s Run Club, which stages nine group runs across the U.S. (and, soon, Europe).

As I watched him that sunny and hot morning, I couldn’t stop thinking: How the hell is this guy still standing, let alone leading a run? It was only Saturday, and Diplo was already deep into a frenzied weekend. He landed in New York City on Thursday morning after taking the overnight flight from his home in Malibu. That evening he DJed from 12:30 a.m. to 3:00 a.m. at the Edge, a venue 100 floors above the city. On Friday, he boarded a seaplane for the Hamptons, where he performed two more sets: a sunset show at Surf Lodge, where Jimmy Buffett and Snoop Dogg have played to crowds of models and billionaires, followed by an impromptu set at Mary Lou’s, a Montauk club on the harbor where he only meant to hang out but ended up taking the decks. He didn’t leave until around 1:00 a.m.

I was at both venues and felt deeply, existentially hungover the next morning. I figured—hoped, really—the run would include some walking. Diplo, however, led the pack. He wore a Whoop, the health tracker with which he has a partnership, and reached a heart rate of 167 beats per minute. “He wasn’t taking it easy at all,” said Greg Grosicki, a staff research scientist at Whoop who reviewed Diplo’s data from his weekend in Montauk.

I didn’t understand how a 47-year-old pulled off this feat—the travel, the DJ sets, the cavorting, the running—without collapsing and retreating to his hotel suite for the rest of the weekend. On Saturday evening he had two more sets, one at the annual gala of the Surfrider Foundation, which supports ocean conservation and includes Sean McPherson and John Slattery as supporters. After that he DJed a private party for investment executive Michael Dorrell before flying private to Ibiza overnight for his next gig.

After the run—which, miraculously, I did finish—I talked with Diplo about how he survives this lifestyle. He even shared his Whoop data with me from the weekend so I could compare his body’s reaction with how he told me he felt. “I’m actually fully cracked out every day, doing way more than running and DJing, more than anybody else,” he said.

He likes to sound nonchalant about it. “When I did an interview with some of the Whoop counselors, they were like, your body is very similar mentally to a Navy SEAL or an ER nurse. You’re able to just get up and go do whatever,” he said. “I can always get up and get shit done, unless I’m sick.” Okay, so maybe Diplo was just born with it. But I learned that he does more for his physical and mental health than he likes to let on. This is the story of how a 47-year-old, internationally renowned DJ, who works and parties into the predawn hours, travels the world, and leads packs of people on runs, pulls it off without coming apart at the seams.

Running appeals to him because it travels well. All you need is a pair of shoes and the will to put them on. “I do things I can do anywhere,” he said. “Running is free.” He aims for 15 miles a week across three or four runs, averaging a seven-and-a-half to eight-minute mile. His fastest mile, six and a half minutes, came after his run club appeared on the prediction platform Polymarket, where people bet against him. “That’s what motivated me to run pretty fast,” he said with a laugh.

DJing counts as cardio too. After all, his sets typically run at least two hours. “It’s a mix of dancing and standing,” he said. “It’s almost like a little air squat.” He’s baffled that his dancers, several from the group Major Lazer, stay in shape without a gym. “I’m like, ‘What do you guys do?’ ” he said. “They’re like, ‘We don’t do anything. We just dance at your shows.’ ”

The numbers back him up: During his Surf Lodge set, his max heart rate hit 117 bpm. “If you consider these sets are two hours long, maintaining a heart rate of 120 is a real physical activity,” Greg Grosicki, the research scientist at Whoop, told me. “It’s equivalent to riding a bike for two hours. You feel pretty wrecked after that, and he’s getting equivalent strain from his sets.”

Diplo mixes cardio and weights in HIIT sessions and does 100 to 200 push-ups a day, several times a week, usually in his hotel room. “It takes five minutes of your life,” he said.

Once a week he wears an electrical muscle stimulation, or EMS, suit for 20 minutes. “It does pulsing with simple moves,” he said, naming a brand called Catalyst and a newer one, Pepper, he’s about to try. He credits the suit, half jokingly, for his arm muscles.

He also takes hot Pilates classes with light weights and works out at Barry’s Bootcamp near his home in Malibu. “There’s an unwritten rule about group fitness in California: You don’t bother celebrities,” he said. “You let them get their job done, then you tell people you saw Chris Martin. Every time I go to Pilates, he’s next to me.”

According to the data, long flights, especially red-eyes, hit Diplo hard, said Grosicki. After an overnight flight to Ibiza, Diplo’s recovery score—a measure of how ready the body is to perform—dropped to 21 percent, and his sleep score to 29 percent. That’s well below average for him. “He’s human, and he’s responding to these stressors,” Grosicki said.

“I do like to get the red-eyes, which probably messes up my sleep the most, but I’d rather be outside in the day,” Diplo said. “Being on a plane during the day is so depressing.” He said he struggles to hold a circadian rhythm and sometimes crashes in the midafternoon. On Thursday, for example, he slept five hours in the middle of the day ahead of his set at the Edge.

Winding down after a set is its own challenge. “I might take a Xanax if I have to,” he said. “I got to stop thinking about things.” He also puts his phone away, listens to audiobooks and history podcasts, skips food before bed (though he does chug electrolytes), and uses PEMF mats, which send low-frequency electromagnetic waves through the body to aid in relaxation. Mostly, though, he just takes what sleep he can get.

Saturday morning, after two Friday-night sets in Montauk, his recovery score was 67 percent and his sleep score 65 percent, both above average. On Monday, after he spent the night in Ibiza, his recovery score was 56 percent and sleep score was 62 percent. As Grosicki put it, “He bounces back.”

Diplo avoids drinking before shows and on travel days, and he hasn’t done recreational drugs in six months. When he does, it’s acid. “I would run on acid, just try things on acid,” he said. “I could fly a plane on acid.”

“Mental health is pretty much everything,” Diplo said. “But you have to get there sometimes by exercising. Finding your body, being in tune with your body, is probably the first thing you can do to have a clear mind, to get rid of any sickness you have, whatever’s keeping you down. That’s the first way to start.”

He’s tried more unconventional resets too. Seven years ago, he smoked toad venom. “I’ll never do it again, but it was pretty hardcore,” he said. “It’s a really big ego death. Being humbled is very good wellness.”

Whatever he’s doing, it seems to be working, at least by the numbers. Whether the rest of us should try it is a different question entirely.

#6863. The Saga of Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Fake Leather Jacket

The Internet loved his outrageous new look. There was just one problem.

There are several ways to respond when you’ve admitted to an affair, your company’s shares are tumbling, and even the White House is discussing your private life. Turning up in a spectacularly studded Saint Laurent leather jacket is one of them. Resigning is another.

For a while, it seemed as if Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old former CEO of Nvidia, had opted for the former. A photograph showing the tech billionaire in an archival Hedi Slimane YSL biker jacket went viral this week. The Internet was delighted. There was just one problem: The photograph was fake.

The resignation, which came just this morning, was real.

As CNN reported, the image had been doctored from a genuine photograph taken at a Seoul airport in June. Nvidia, which one might imagine has other things to deal with right now, confirmed it wasn’t real.

But perhaps the reason so many people believed it was that Huang already dresses like this. Leather jackets are his uniform. He reportedly owns 30 or 40 of them, including a snazzy reptile-effect number worn to deliver his company’s keynote at the Consumer Electronics Show.

And Hedi Slimane was the perfect designer to bring into the fantasy. The Frenchman, who ran Saint Laurent from 2012 to 2016, made his name dressing skinny rock stars and turning their disheveled, devil-may-care attitude—later rebranded as so-called “indie sleaze”—into expensive luxury fashion. His leather jackets were practically a uniform for men who were determined to look as though they didn’t care what anyone thought and/or having a midlife crisis.

For a billionaire in the middle of a spectacularly public scandal, it was quite a look. One Instagram commenter described Huang as the first person to achieve “negative aura” in archival Hedi.

There’s another irony. Huang has previously said his wife, Lori—i.e., the wronged party in all this—helps choose his clothes.

And then there’s the technology itself. Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution, including the tools capable of ... producing convincing fake photographs.

In conclusion, then, the image wasn’t real. But as a portrait of a billionaire in the middle of a spectacularly public crisis, we so wanted it to be.

#6862. Before Anything Else, Geoffrey Holder Was a Painter. A New Show Spotlights His Tremendous Body of Work

Geoffrey Holder refused to choose a lane. Born in Trinidad and Tobago in 1930, he was a principal dancer with the Metropolitan Opera Ballet, the first Black man to win Tony Awards for both directing and costume design (for the Broadway hit The Wiz), and the voice and face of 7Up throughout the 1970s and ’80s, all while building a celebrated film career with roles in Doctor Dolittle, Annie, and the Bond film Live and Let Die.

And yet, before everything else, Holder was a painter. “Painting always came first,” says his son, Leo Holder, who oversees the artist’s estate. “Practically everything else he did has always been an extension of this. He was always working on something. At any given time, wherever he was living, there were several canvases in progress.” Still, across his decades-long career, it was the facet of his work that received the least attention.

“Geoffrey Holder: Black Magic,” on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art North Miami from November 18, 2026, to April 4, 2027, aims to correct this. Guest curated by Dr. Erica Moiah James, principal investigator and publication editor for the Geoffrey Holder Project, it’s the first museum survey to center Holder’s work as a visual artist. Bringing together more than 60 works across eight decades, the show offers an unprecedented look at the practice that anchored his entire multidisciplinary career.

Geoffrey Holder, Untitled, n.d. Oil, oil marker, and China marker on wood. 84 x 36 inches.

Influenced by his older brother, Boscoe Holder—himself a painter, designer, dancer, and musician—Geoffrey took up painting in childhood and had his first formal exhibition in Trinidad by the age of 14. According to his son, Holder funded his move to the United States in the early 1950s by selling 20 of his paintings, and when he died in 2014, he left behind more than 250 paintings and 300 collages, along with a trove of drawings, sculptures, and photographs.

The exhibition is the result of more than a decade of work, beginning when James was first invited by Holder’s family to see his archive in 2015. “I knew Geoffrey the way most people knew him,” James tells Vogue. “I had seen his films. I knew he was involved with The Wiz, I had seen the 7Up commercials. But I didn’t know him. What I realized the moment I stepped into his archive is that he knew himself. He understood there would be a moment when people would get it. He might not be there, but he was going to select and preserve the record of his life so that we could really dive into it.”

Geoffrey Holder, Waiting for the Dance, 2001. Oil, pastel crayon, and China marker on Masonite. 48 x 48 inches unframed. 50 ½ x 50 ½ inches framed.

The show takes its title from Holder’s deep interest in what he dubbed “magical people,” those whose creative spirit and sheer presence carried an unmistakable energy. “There’s a negative way of framing Black people as ‘magical Negroes,’ but he wasn’t thinking that way,” James explains. “He thought of it in incredibly positive terms, and was referencing a je ne sais quoi—something almost beyond language, a sort of confidence and way of being in the world that is truly remarkable. So we took the word ‘magic’ and racialized it, because most of the subjects in the exhibition are Black people.”

Occupying the full museum, the show is organized into five sections—Portraits, Epistles, The Sacred and the Profane, Genre, and Figure Studies—pairing the artworks with a rich collection of costume sketches, performance footage, correspondence, and memorabilia that provide historical context while illustrating the breadth and depth of Holder’s creative life.

One standout is Portrait of Carmen (1980), an oil on canvas depicting a stylized Black woman in a sleek black dress and turquoise earrings against a crimson background. The painting reflects not only Holder’s interest in the female figure but also his profound devotion to his wife, the American dancer, choreographer, and actress Carmen de Lavallade, to whom he was married for 59 years, until his death. Also on view is the portrait Woman in Yellow (1985), part of a motif that, according to James, traces back to the first time Holder saw de Lavallade, wearing a yellow dress. “He painted women in various stages of a yellow dress forever,” she says.

Geoffrey Holder and Carmen de Lavallade in 1955, the year they married.

Also central to the show is a series of works that reinterpret biblical stories through Holder’s distinctive lens. Adam and Eve (ca. 1990s), for instance, is a towering diptych in oil, oil marker, and china marker on canvas, in which black tree trunks rise through a dense forest of green leaves; in the lower left corner, two nude figures are nearly swallowed by the foliage. In another large oil painting, Adam and Eve (2000–2005), Holder returns to the same subject, this time creating a more intimate image that foregrounds the couple while still enveloping them in greenery. Holder’s son explains that the artist’s interest in biblical narratives was not, strictly speaking, religious. Instead, “he saw them as a wonderful source of storytelling, theater, and drama.”

Geoffrey Holder, Adam and Eve, 2000-2005. Oil on board. 71 7/8 x 30 inches unframed. 73 ½ x 31 ¼ inches framed.

In another biblically inspired work, John the Baptist and Jesus (undated), Holder depicts the two figures as Black men standing together in cerulean water, sharing a tender moment as a crowd looks on. “This is one of my favorites, because it shows a level of intimacy between Black men—a level of care, gentleness, and tenderness that you just don’t [usually] see out in the world,” James says. “Geoffrey is making a point. He’s appropriating the religious story, but there’s something very contemporary, maybe even a longing for that kind of open expression of care among Black men in the world.”

Reflecting on the interest in his father’s visual art practice more than a decade after his death, Leo Holder says he’s more convinced than ever that, as a multihyphenate, his father was ahead of his time, rarely seen as a serious painter because of his many other creative pursuits. “Nowadays, we have far more of an ecosystem that allows you to be polymathic. And he’s gotten the kind of attention for his art that he never got when he was alive,” he says. “In part, it’s because now everybody’s caught up.”

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The latest AirTags, MacBooks, and AirPods are up to 23 percent off.

Our editors look forward to rare discounts on Apple devices every Black Friday, and this year is no exception. Leading up to Amazon’s official sale (which runs from November 19 to 30), we’re already seeing up to 23 percent off Apple’s most coveted tech.

All to say, if you want to get a head start on shopping, there are plenty of options available now. Ahead, see what we’re adding to our carts from Apple this Black Friday.

Lost luggage is a thing of the past with Apple’s ingenious AirTags, which give you peace of mind by tracking the location of your prized possessions. Snag one for a record-low price of $23 ahead of Black Friday.

Apple’s AirPods Pro are worth the hype. Complete with features like Active Noise Cancellation and transparency modes, a water-resistant design, and silicone ear tips for a customizable fit, they’re bound to become your daily headphones. Currently, they’re at a typical sale price of $199, but they’ve been as low as $169 during past sales.

Get $250 off the latest version of the MacBook Air. This 13-inch computer weighs just 2.7 pounds and boasts up to 18 hours of battery life, making it easy to tote to and from work, class, your local coffee shop—you name it.

Everyone deserves a pair of headphones that are as chic as they are functional. If you prefer an over-ear style, add this highly covetable pair to your cart, as they tend to sell out quickly when they’re on sale. We expect even steeper savings once Black Friday arrives, but you’ve got a better chance of securing a pair if you shop now.

The 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple’s most sophisticated laptop, is a worthy splurge, even at full price. Updated with an ultra-quick M5 chip, this computer boasts enhanced graphics and a speedier performance than past models. Plus, it boasts a Liquid Retina display for crystal-clear imagery, an all-day battery, and built-in AI tech.

Ahead of Black Friday, the standard iPad is $49 off. Though this is an entry-level option, it boasts features like Touch ID, a 10-hour battery life, and an impressive 11.2-inch Liquid Retina display.

Whether you’re new to the world of wearables or need to upgrade an older device, the Apple Watch SE makes it easy to do so without breaking the bank. It’s not on sale yet, but it was at a record-low price of $199 in July, so we’re expecting a similar price once November 27 comes.

Don’t let this tablet’s tiny size fool you: This is the perfect device for watching Netflix on the go, devouring your latest literary fiction read, or jotting down notes during flights. It’s only $30 off right now, but it was on sale for a record-low price of $349 last Black Friday.

#6858. The 17 Best Comedy Movies of 2026

Thanks to The Invite, Coyote vs. Acme, and Stop! That! Train!, big-screen comedy is making a comeback.

Are comedies making a comeback? Over the past decade, you couldn’t get a laugh into theaters even if it was forced. Hollywood decided that comedies weren’t worth the same treatment as superhero tentpoles or low-budget horror, and just about every legacy franchise sequel of a former ‘90s comedy disappointed audiences because they were basically cash grabs that played on nostalgia. Comedy needed help.

So, in 2026, some fresh films forced Hollywood to come to its senses. Coyote vs. Acme, a Looney Tunes film that Warner Bros. originally dropped to claim a tax write-off, grossed over $126 million at the box office. Olivia Wilde’s The Invite might just receive nominations for every major award category at the Oscars, and Airplane!-esque humor made a comeback in RuPaul’s hilarious disaster flick Stop! That! Train!

If you’re in need of a belly laugh, check out the best comedies of 2026 below.

Don’t get me wrong, Coyote vs. Acme is no Space Jam. But the Looney Tunes film that triumphantly won the box office—even after Warner Bros. gave up on it—is still one of the funniest movies of the year. The story follows Wile E. Coyote as he partners with a lowly injury attorney (Will Forte) to sue the ACME Corporation for its defective products. The comedy also stars John Cena as ACME’s defense attorney, who probably has the funniest line of the year when he tells Tweety Bird: “I don’t pay you to tink you taw, I pay you to taw.”

Olivia Colman stars in this romantic comedy drama about a lonely fisherwoman who grows tired of the town’s harassment due to her smell. So, she asks a magical basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband (Alexander Skarsgård) out of wicker. What follows is a bizarre yet hilarious story about the follies of marriage, jealousy, and tons of sex with a man made out of basket material.

Sam Rockwell leads this sci-fi comedy by former Pirates of the Caribbean director Gore Verbinski, about a time-traveler who travels to the same diner over and over again in a Groundhog Day–esque loop because he believes that if he can take the right configuration of people from the diner back to the future with him then he may be able to save the world from AI’s takeover. I know, it’s strange. But Verbinski makes the comedy work, especially when you learn about each diner patron via small vignettes emphasizing various doomsday scenarios.

Real estate agent Rudd Landy (John Cena) is called to the hospital when his brother gets into a car accident. Turns out, the man in emergency care is not his real brother (Christopher Meloni), but someone that he used to mentor when he was younger as part of a Big Brothers Big Sisters program. Without anywhere else to go, Rudd agrees to help take care of his “little brother” (Eric André) while he recovers, even if his little brother might just ruin his life.

When Gail Daughtry’s (Zoey Deutch) husband takes their celebrity sex pass joke literally, Gail sets out to get even by tracking down her celebrity sex pass—John Hamm—to have sex with him and even out the score. The comedy film also stars “Weird Al” Yankovic, Ben Wang, Sabrina Impacciatore, Joe Lo Truglio, Fred Melamed, and Mad Men’s John Slattery as himself.

Johnny Knoxville, Steve-O, and the whole Jackass crew return for one last ride in Jackass: Best and Last, another compilation of skits, stunts, and pranks from some of the most fearless people on the planet. They hit each other in the groin with wooden mallets, hook their penises up to shock collars, and reminisce about some of their most iconic sketches throughout the years.

Half RuPaul’s Drag Race, half Airplane! for Bravo fans, Stop! That! Train! is the dumbest movie I’ve seen all year (complimentary). The film follows RuPaul and her Drag Race stars as they attempt to stop a speeding bullet train heading straight toward the storm of the century, aka a Stormaganza. Even if you’re so out of your depth that you have no idea what’s going on, Stop! That! Train! argues that that’s okay. It’s comedy for comedy’s sake, and we need more of that at the theater.

Mel Brooks just turned 100 years old (!!!). But before that, he was 99 in Mel Brooks: The 99-Year-Old Man!—a two-part HBO documentary directed by Judd Apatow. The film, which chronicles the comedian’s career throughout The Producers, Blazing Saddles, Spaceballs, Young Frankenstein, and many more, also touches on his work as a film producer. Still, it’s the testimonies from his friendship with Carl Reiner and his marriage to Anne Bancroft that really pull at the heartstrings after a good laugh down memory lane.

Olivia Wilde is not afraid of Virginia Woolf. In the actress’s latest film, The Invite, the classic dinner-party setup full of playful talking and relationship arguments somehow morphs into a sex comedy. The whole film takes place in Angela (Wilde) and Joe’s (Seth Rogen) apartment as they welcome the raucous upstairs neighbors Pina (Penelope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton). But unlike Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? and its descent into anger and grief, The Invite asks more questions about love, commitment, and everyone’s stance on orgies.

The struggling music duo always works for me. Whether it’s Flight of the Conchords or Ishtar, there’s something funny about people with no talent still trying to make it to the top. Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie takes the genre to maybe its lowest budget yet, as the Canadian web-series comedians somehow also make room to spoof Back to the Future and incorporate real Nathan Fielder–like guerrilla filmmaking.

One of the coolest movies to premiere out of SXSW was the Hulu original Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice, from writer/director BenDavid Grabinski. A loan shark (Vince Vaughn) uses a time machine to undo one bad night involving his close friend (James Marsden) and his wife (Eiza González). Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice is the kind of movie you want when the pizza is hot, the beers are cold, and your friends are indecisive about what you all want to watch.

After years of creative and financial slump, Pixar has found its groove again with Hoppers. Essentially Animal Farm meets Avatar, Hoppers tells the story of a genius college student whose participation in a breakthrough science experiment lets her become a beaver who can communicate with animals. Though her efforts to help animals seem promising at first, she quickly realizes what really happens when animals (and bugs!) fight back against mankind. Directed by We Bare Bears creator Daniel Chong, Hoppers is an easygoing, family-friendly romp through the wilderness.

Liam Neeson continues his funny streak in the action comedy Cold Storage. Joe Keery (Stranger Things) plays a slacker employee of a storage facility who, along with his cute coworker (Georgina Campbell), discovers a deadly, mutating fungus. Teaming up with a grizzled federal agent (Neeson), the three work to save the world. Basically a modern-day Outbreak, Cold Storage isn’t one to leave dormant on your watch list.

Dave Bautista and Jason Momoa make up the ultimate action-movie tag team in The Wrecking Crew. The guys play estranged brothers in Hawaii who work together to piece together who killed their father and how on earth the Japanese yakuza is involved.

Boots Riley, the writer and director of Sorry to Bother You, does it again with his crime caper I Love Boosters. In this anticapitalist satire, a crew of professional thieves works to take down a ruthless fashion giant (Demi Moore). Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige, Poppy Liu, Eiza González, and more make up this delirious ensemble that takes Ocean’s Eleven and dresses it in hyper-surreal shades.

Sometimes we need a nauseatingly cute rom-com. Kevin James (yes, The King of Queens) stars in this breezy and uplifting comedy about a man who, after being left at the altar, goes on his Italian honeymoon solo. While there, he makes new friends and even deeper connections with strangers halfway around the world. A feel-good flick about new beginnings, Solo Mio can lift you high when you’re feeling down.

A stoner comedy? In 2026? In this economy? Well, the streaming generation can finally know what it’s like to have their own Harold & Kumar with Pizza Movie. Gaten Matarazzo and Sean Giambrone star as college roommates and social pariahs who, while high on a new hallucinogenic drug, embark on a psychedelic odyssey to make it downstairs and get their pizza delivery. Despite a popular meme mocking the movie’s marketing, Pizza Movie performed well with critics at its SXSW premiere.

#6857. 13 Fab Old Photos of 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Inductee Sade Adu

Think Sade, and a few things likely pop to mind. There’s the signature beauty look: the dark eyeliner, shapely brows, red lip, and long, slicked-back plait. There are the clothes: good earrings—often big gold hoops—and stage outfits that were sexy, yes, but also slyly demure; high-waisted trousers, semi-sheer turtlenecks, cropped jackets, qipao-style dresses. You may nerdily make the distinction between Sade the woman—Helen Folasade Adu, OBE, born on January 16, 1959, in Ibadan, Nigeria—and Sade the Grammy-winning band, formed in 1982 and made up of Adu, Paul Denman, Andrew Hale, and Stuart Matthewman.

Now there’s one more thing to add to that list: the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. This weekend, the band will celebrate their induction—along with acts including Phil Collins, Billy Idol, Oasis, and the late Luther Vandross—in a ceremony at Los Angeles’s Peacock Theater. Now, will any of Sade’s members actually be present for that ceremony? No, according to a statement released on November 10. Even so, they called the recognition “both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks, not only to those who voted for us but also every single person who lets our music into their lives.”

And what music that is: from “Smooth Operator” to “Kiss of Life,” “Is It a Crime” to “No Ordinary Love,” “The Sweetest Taboo” to “I Couldn’t Love You More,” Sade’s soulful, sui generis sound remains a benchmark for timeless cool.

Here, in celebration of her group’s latest honor, we’ve rounded up 13 striking old photographs of the divine Sade Adu, a generational talent and forever style icon.

Sporting spotty shirting, high-waisted trousers, and a wide belt during a 1984 set in Rotterdam.

This is no ordinary love–and those are no ordinary neutrals. A graduate of London’s Saint Martin’s School of Art, Sade shows off her style bonafides at the Hammersmith Odeon in 1984.

Cooler than cool in sunglasses and a simple white button-down.

Performing at the Live Aid charity concert at Wembley Stadium in 1985.

Gold jewelry, jaunty bolero jacket, can’t lose.

In textured whites—and that classic red lip—at the Ambassador East Hotel in Chicago, 1985.

Making her Saturday Night Live debut on December 14, 1985, with Tom Hanks as host. The band performed “Is It a Crime” and “The Sweetest Taboo,” both from their second studio album, Promise.

In 2010, recalling the release of Sade’s debut album, Diamond Life, in 1984, The New Yorker’s Sasha Frere-Jones poetically described Adu’s voice on as “a grainy contralto full of air that betrays a slight ache but no agony, and values even imperfect dignity over a show of pain.”

Center-stage at at Northrop Auditorium in Minneapolis, 1993.

With the English singer-songwriter Leo Sayer at a charity ball in London, 2001.

Having a moment at the United Center in Chicago, 2001.

Red all over, in concert at PNC Bank Arts Center in Holmdel, New Jersey, 2001.

#6855. I Can Feel the Tremors of History Rumbling Beneath Scott Colom’s Victory

The senator-elect from Mississippi invoked Medger Evers in his winning speech, which reminded me of how far we’ve come—and how far we still have to go.

(Optional Musical Accompaniment to This Post)

Okay! Now we can celebrate. From the Mississippi Free Press:

Oh, to hell with the numbers. Let’s just celebrate a win by a guy cool enough to receive the good news of his election while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. From his victory speech:

One day in 1994, in the employ of another magazine, I went down to Jackson on assignment for a story about the death penalty that ultimately never ran. It was the day after the Republicans, led by Representative Newt Gingrich, won control of the entire Congress for the first time since 1952 and control of the House of Representatives for the first time since 1954. It can be argued, and I have, that these results scared the courage out of the Democratic party as thoroughly as George McGovern’s landslide loss to Richard Nixon in 1972 did. And when the modern Democratic party gets scared, it inevitably runs away from its most sacred commitments and the proudest moments in its history. This result caused Democratic president Bill Clinton to sign grotesque legislation like the Defense of Marriage Act and a crime bill that, relevant to my mission to Mississippi, added 28 new death-penalty crimes to the federal code. The bar in the Walthall Hotel, where I was staying, was filled every night by gloating Republicans, which drove me to room service for the balance of my stay.

On my last day in Jackson, I took a drive across town to what was then called 2332 Guynes Street in the Elraine subdivision, which had been developed in the 1950s by men named Winston Thompson and Leroy Burnett in order to service the rising Black middle class of the city. One of the houses in the development was purchased by Medgar and Myrlie Evers. On the night of June 12, 1963, Myrlie and their children were watching the speech in which President John F. Kennedy finally got off the dime on civil rights when they heard Medgar’s car coming up the driveway. The kids ran out to greet him. From behind a bush across the street, a back-shooting coward named Byron De La Beckwith sighted down his .30–06 Enfield and murdered Medgar Evers in front of his family.

I parked my car and walked slowly from De La Beckwith’s sniper’s nest to the driveway at 2332 Guynes Street, tracing the route of the bullet that killed Medgar Evers on that night in 1963. I was strangely aware of every step I took. I was deeply aware of the rise and fall of my feet, one after the other. It was as though there were a tiny tremor of history beneath me the closer I came to the spot under the carport where he fell, bleeding, before his family. It felt very much like a pilgrimage to some ancient shrine. There were sad and solemn bells tolling in my mind.

Listening to Scott Colom accept his victory on Wednesday night, as he name-checked Medgar Evers, along with Fannie Lou Hamer and Hiram Revels, I heard those bells again in my mind. Loud and raucous this time, they drowned out the crack of the whip and the crack of a .30–06 Enfield rifle fired with murderous intent. This time, they rang with joy, and the tremors of history I felt beneath my feet that day in 1994 felt like an earthquake.
